record.paper_title: Negative (and Positive) Circles in Signed Graphs: A Problem Collection
record.original_question: For a signed digraph (D, σ), determine when the directed frustration index—the minimum number of edges whose deletion makes the digraph cycle balanced—equals the ordinary frustration index of the underlying undirected signed graph.

evidence.quote: Qn. 1− What is the directed frustration index l(D, σ), i.e., the smallest number of edges whose deletion results in cycle balance? ... therefore the directed frustration index is bounded above by the undirected frustration index l(Γ, σ), where Γ is the undirected underlying graph of D. Under what conditions are they equal?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $D=(V,E)$ be a digraph and let $\sigma:E\to\{+1,-1\}$ be a sign function on its arcs, so that $(D,\sigma)$ is a signed digraph. The sign of a directed cycle in $D$ is the product of the signs of its arcs. The signed digraph $(D,\sigma)$ is called cycle balanced if every directed cycle of $D$ is positive (i.e., has sign $+1$). Define the directed frustration index
$$\ell(D,\sigma) := \min\{|F| : F\subseteq E,\ (D-F,\sigma) \text{ is cycle balanced}\}.$$
Let $\Gamma$ denote the underlying undirected graph of $D$, with the induced edge signs, and let $\ell(\Gamma,\sigma)$ denote its (undirected) frustration index, i.e., the minimum number of edges whose deletion yields a balanced signed graph (one in which every undirected cycle is positive). It is known that $\ell(D,\sigma)\le \ell(\Gamma,\sigma)$.

Determine necessary and sufficient combinatorial conditions on $(D,\sigma)$ under which
$$\ell(D,\sigma) = \ell(\Gamma,\sigma).$$
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in a problem collection on signed graphs and circles. No subsequent paper appears to provide a characterization of when the directed frustration index of a signed digraph equals the undirected frustration index of its underlying signed graph; related works on frustration index of signed (di)graphs continue to study computation and bounds rather than this specific equality condition.
